summary: Describes how Mobile IPv6 bootstrapping uses a Diameter Network Access Server to interact with Diameter servers, so home agent address, home address and security details can be provided dynamically through existing AAA infrastructure. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone roams onto a network, it needs to be told which home agent to register with and which home network prefix to use. This RFC lets the network's access server ask the operator's authentication server for those details while the phone is signing in, instead of having them built into the device.

questions: diameter nas to aaa for mipv6
how does a mobile node get a home agent
subtitle: How a network access server gets a mobile IPv6 home agent address from the operator's authentication server.

tldr.problem: A mobile node must register with a home agent, but it needs to know the home agent's address, the home link prefix and other parameters before it can do so, and configuring those on every device is an administrative burden.
tldr.mechanism: New Diameter attribute-value pairs carry the home agent address, the home agent's realm and host, the home link prefix and a feature vector, so the access server can obtain them during the normal access authentication exchange.
tldr.outcome: The home agent can be chosen dynamically, either by the operator's Diameter server or by a local one, and the RFC sets out how the two sides agree on which is used.

today: RFC 5447 is a Proposed Standard from February 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines one new Diameter AVP, two AVPs taken from the RADIUS attribute space so that they work over RADIUS as well, and a new registry of mobility capability flags.

sections.title: Why a Mobile Node Needs a Home Agent Address
sections.content:
The Mobile IPv6 specification requires a mobile node to perform registration with a home agent with information about its current point of attachment, the care-of address. The home agent creates and maintains the binding between the mobile node's home address and its care-of address.

In order to register with a home agent, the mobile node needs information such as the home link prefix, the home agent address, the home address or addresses, the home link prefix length, and security-association-related information. That information may be statically configured, but static provisioning becomes an administrative burden for an operator. It also does not address load balancing, failover, opportunistic home link assignment, or assignment of local home agents in close proximity to the mobile node, and the ability to react to sudden environmental or topological changes is minimal.

Dynamic assignment of MIPv6 home registration information is therefore desirable for ease of deployment and network maintenance. The AAA infrastructure, which is used for access authentication, can be leveraged to assign some or all of the necessary parameters. The Diameter server in the access service provider's or mobility service provider's network may return these parameters to the AAA client, which might be either the Network Access Server in the integrated scenario or the home agent in the split scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: A roaming device cannot work out for itself where its home agent is. Handing it out at sign-in time means the operator can move that work around, fail over, and pick a home agent near the device, instead of baking the answer into every handset.

sections.title: The Players
sections.content:
An Access Service Authorizer is a network operator that authenticates a mobile node and establishes the node's authorization to receive Internet service. The Access Service Provider is a network operator that provides direct IP packet forwarding to and from the mobile node.

A Mobility Service Authorizer is a service provider that authorizes MIPv6 service, and the Mobility Service Provider is a service provider that provides it. In order to obtain such service, the mobile node must be authenticated and authorized to do so.

A Network Access Server is a device that provides an access service for a user to a network. The Home AAA server is an authentication, authorization and accounting server located in the user's home network, in the home realm. The Local AAA server is a proxy in the local access service provider's network, and the Visited AAA server is a proxy in a visited network. In a roaming case the local Diameter proxy has the visited AAA role.

In the split scenario, the mobility service and the network access service are authorized by different entities. In the integrated scenario, they are authorized by the same entity, and MIPv6 bootstrapping is provided as part of the network access authentication procedure. This document focuses on the integrated scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: The access server sits in the network the device has just joined. The home server sits in the network the device belongs to. The RFC describes the case where the same organisation handles both, so one sign-in covers network access and mobility service.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Flow
sections.content:
This document addresses the AAA functionality required for the MIPv6 bootstrapping solutions, and focuses on the Diameter-based AAA functionality for the NAS-to-HAAA server communication. In the integrated scenario, MIPv6 bootstrapping is provided as part of the network access authentication procedure.

In a typical MIPv6 access scenario, the mobile node is attached to an access service provider's network. During the network attachment procedure the mobile node interacts with the NAS, which acts as a Diameter client. Subsequently the NAS interacts with the Diameter server over the NAS-to-HAAA interface.

When the Diameter server performs the authentication and authorization for network access, it also determines whether the user is authorized for the MIPv6 service. Based on the MIPv6 service authorization and the user's policy profile, the Diameter server may return several MIPv6 bootstrapping-related parameters to the NAS. The interface described here is not tied to DHCPv6 as the only mechanism to convey MIPv6-related configuration parameters from the NAS to the mobile node.

While this specification addresses the bootstrapping of home agent information and possibly the assignment of the home link prefix, it does not address how the security association between the mobile node and the home agent is created. The creation or use of that security association takes place after the procedures described here, and is therefore out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange happens while the device is signing in to the network. The access server passes on what the device told it, and the operator's server answers with the home agent details, if the subscription allows MIPv6. Setting up the secure tunnel between the device and the home agent is a later step that this RFC does not cover.

sections.title: The MIP6-Agent-Info AVP
sections.content:
The MIP6-Agent-Info AVP, code 486, is of type Grouped and contains the information needed to assign a home agent to the mobile node. When it is present in a message it must contain either the MIP-Home-Agent-Address AVP, the MIP-Home-Agent-Host AVP, or both. The grouped AVP allows up to two home agent addresses, which is useful for deployments where the home agent has both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, and particularly for Dual Stack Mobile IPv6 deployments.

If both the address and the host AVPs are present, the address AVP should have precedence over the host AVP, because the address points to a specific home agent whereas the host may point to a group of home agents in the same realm. The host AVP is of type Grouped and contains both the Destination-Realm and the Destination-Host AVPs of the home agent. Its use is equivalent to the address AVP but offers an additional level of indirection by using the DNS infrastructure: the Destination-Host identifies a home agent and the Destination-Realm identifies the realm where it is located. It is recommended that the host AVP is always included in the MIP6-Agent-Info AVP, so that the home agent can be associated with the realm of the Diameter entity that added it.

The MIP6-Agent-Info AVP may also be attached by the NAS or by the intermediating Diameter proxies in a request message as a hint of a locally assigned home agent, and by the proxies in a reply message if locally assigned home agents are authorized by the Diameter server. There may be multiple instances of it in Diameter messages, for example where the NAS receives home agent information from the mobile node's home network and locally allocated home agent information from the visited network. An NAS should therefore expect to receive multiple MIP6-Agent-Info AVPs.
sections.plainLanguage: One grouped attribute carries the home agent details. It can name the home agent by address, by the realm and host name where DNS can find it, or both. It can appear more than once in a message, so a client must be ready for that.

sections.title: The Home Link Prefix and the Feature Vector
sections.content:
The MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix AVP, code 125, is of type OctetString and contains the Mobile IPv6 home network prefix information in network byte order. The home network prefix must be encoded as the 8-bit prefix length information, one octet, followed by the 128-bit field, 16 octets, for the available home network prefix. The trailing bits of the IPv6 prefix after the prefix length bits must be set to zero, so with a prefix length of 60 the remaining 68 bits must be zero.

The home AAA server may act as a central entity managing prefixes for mobile nodes, in which case it returns the prefix allocated to the node and the NAS delivers it to the node. The NAS may propose a specific prefix to allocate by including the AVP in the request, but the home AAA server may override that hint and return a different prefix.

The MIP6-Feature-Vector AVP, code 124, is of type Unsigned64 and contains a 64-bit flags field of supported capabilities of the NAS or access service provider. Sending and receiving it with the value 0 must be supported, although that does not provide much guidance about specific needs of bootstrapping. The NAS may include it to indicate its capabilities, for example that a local home agent can be provided, and the Diameter server may include it to say which of those capabilities are supported or authorized.

Two capabilities are defined. MIP6_INTEGRATED, value 1, means that the integrated scenario bootstrapping functionality is supported, whether set by the NAS or by the Diameter server. LOCAL_HOME_AGENT_ASSIGNMENT, value 2, means that a local home agent outside the home realm is requested and may be assigned to the mobile node; when set by the Diameter server in the answer message, the assignment of local home agents is authorized. A local home agent may be assigned by the NAS, the local AAA server or the visited AAA server depending on the network architecture and the deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Two more attributes travel with the reply. One carries the home network prefix, with its length in the first byte and the rest padded with zeroes. The other is a bit field of capabilities, so the access server can say it can offer a local home agent and the operator's server can say whether that is allowed.

sections.title: Three Ways to Assign a Home Agent
sections.content:
In the first scenario the NAS allocates a local home agent itself and tells the Diameter server which address it chose, with the address 2001:db8:1:c020::1 in the example. The request carries the MIP6-Feature-Vector with the LOCAL_HOME_AGENT_ASSIGNMENT and MIP6_INTEGRATED flags set, and the MIP6-Agent-Info AVP containing the proposed address. Depending on the Diameter server's configuration and the user's subscription profile, the server either accepts or rejects the local home agent; in the example it accepts and returns the same two flags.

In the second scenario the NAS supports the integrated scenario but does not offer local home agent assignment, so only the MIP6_INTEGRATED flag is set. The Diameter server allocates a home agent and conveys the address, 2001:db8:6000:302::1 in the example, in the MIP-Home-Agent-Address AVP.

In the third scenario the NAS says it can assign a local home agent, and the Diameter server both provides a home agent and authorizes the local one, so the answer carries both home agents. Whether the NAS then offers the locally assigned home agent or the one from the Diameter server is, in this example, based on the local policy. If the Diameter server does not allow the mobile node to use a locally assigned home agent, it returns the feature vector with the LOCAL_HOME_AGENT_ASSIGNMENT bit unset and the home agent address it allocated.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three shapes of answer. The operator's server can hand out the home agent itself, the visited network can hand out a local one with the operator's permission, or the operator's server can hand out one and also allow the local one. The bit in the feature vector says which is allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the Diameter interaction required to accomplish the integrated scenario are described in the integrated-scenario document. The security considerations for the Diameter base protocol, the Diameter NASREQ application and the Diameter EAP application, with respect to network access authentication and the transport of keying material, are also applicable to this document. Developers should ensure that special attention is paid to configuring the security associations protecting the messages that enable the global positioning and allocation of home agents.

Furthermore, the Diameter messages may be transported between the NAS and the Diameter server via one or more AAA brokers or Diameter agents such as proxies. In that case the AAA communication from the NAS to the Diameter server relies on the security properties of the intermediate brokers and agents.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange that tells the network where the home agent is must be protected, and if it passes through proxy servers, the protection depends on every hop in between.

viz.caption: THE BOOTSTRAPPING EXCHANGE; ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC

messages.label: IEEE 802.1X, PANA, IKEv2, DHCP
messages.note: The mobile node attaches to the network.

messages.label: DIAMETER-EAP-REQUEST
messages.note: Carries the feature vector and, if the NAS picked one, a proposed home agent address.

messages.label: DIAMETER-EAP-ANSWER
messages.note: Returns the home agent information the server authorized.

viz.caption: THE ATTRIBUTE-VALUE PAIRS THIS DOCUMENT USES

items.label: MIP6-Agent-Info
items.desc: Grouped attribute holding the home agent information.

items.label: MIP-Home-Agent-Address
items.desc: The IPv6 or IPv4 address of the home agent.

items.label: MIP-Home-Agent-Host
items.desc: The realm and host name of the home agent.

items.label: MIP6-Home-Link-Prefix
items.desc: The home network prefix, with its length in the first octet.

items.label: MIP6-Feature-Vector
items.desc: A 64-bit flags field of supported capabilities.

viz.caption: WHAT THE ANSWER MEANS IN EACH CASE, AS SEEN BY THE NAS

cells: No home agent assignment allowed by the home or visited AAA server.
A local home agent is not allowed. The home AAA server assigns a home agent in the home network.
A local home agent is allowed. No home or visited AAA server assigned a home agent.
A local home agent is allowed and the visited AAA server assigns one.
A local home agent is allowed and the home AAA server also assigns one.

viz.caption: THE TWO CAPABILITY FLAGS IN THE FEATURE VECTOR

items.title: MIP6_INTEGRATED
items.text: Set when the integrated scenario bootstrapping is supported, by the access server or by the Diameter server.

items.title: LOCAL_HOME_AGENT_ASSIGNMENT
items.text: Set when a local home agent outside the home realm is requested, or when the Diameter server authorizes one.
